NVIDIA is investigating an alleged relationship between its CEO and a Chinese businesswoman
who is accused of spying for China.
And here's Rebecca Hersher reports.
The statement by NVIDIA's board of directors cites recent reporting by the New York Times,
which alleges that the CEO of NVIDIA, Jensen Huang, had a close relationship with a woman
named Alice Huang.
The two are not related.
Times reporter Anna Swanson discussed the reporting on NPR technology podcast MachineGods.
So Alice Huang is a Chinese national.
She's a Chinese businesswoman who had something of kind of a mysterious and meteoric rise.
The reporting by The Times suggests Huang may have helped China get around U.S. limits
on exports of powerful AI chips.
Republican lawmakers have asked NVIDIA's CEO to appear before Congress to address the allegations.
Rebecca Hersher, NPR News.
New White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller, starts his new job tomorrow, taking over from

This has Democrats promised investigations into the administration when they take control
of both chambers of Congress in January.
Incoming House oversight chairman Congressman Robert Garcia warned Trump officials to "lawyer
up."
Attorney General Todd Blanche.
My job is if they try to come after Stephen Miller for these, whatever it is that Garcia
thinks he's going to do, instead of actually just conducting oversight and leading.
Of course, the Department of Justice will be there to defend him, just like if they
went after any cabinet secretary or any person in government.
We do it all the time.
Speaking there to CNN's State of the Union.

of staff, but rather he swore an oath to the United States Constitution."
Floodwaters have receded across Southwest Colorado, but residents are just starting to take stock
of all the damage after back-to-back floods.
Colorado Public Radio's Tina Sigra reports in Archuleta County, officials say at least
700 homes have been impacted.
Many are around the small town of Pagosa Springs, where the San Juan River nearly hit a historic
high November 1, more than four feet above major flood stage.
Medical Pastor John Duncan with Center Point Church has been helping residents.
He says they're resilient, but many are overwhelmed.
It's just heartbreaking as you watch the memories of your children and the treasures that you've
kept floating around in your house completely ruined.
Duncan is hosting dozens of out-of-town church members helping clean up the devastation.
For NPR News, I'm Tina Sig in Grand Junction, Colorado.
And you're listening to NPR News from Washington.
The strong earthquake hit central Japan early today, injuring at least 22 people.
Empiers Anthony Kuhn reports authorities are warning of strong aftershocks in the coming
days.
The quake hit just after 1 a.m. local time and was centered on central Shizuoka Prefecture
at a depth of 25 miles below the Earth's surface.
Japan's meteorological agency put it at magnitude 5.7, the U.S. Geological Survey at 5.5.
The quake threw some of the injured off stairs or from their beds.
It shattered windows and sent merchandise tumbling from store shelves.
Authorities reported that following the quake, no changes were detected in the Nankai Troff,
a fault line running along Japan's east coast.
Authorities put the chance of a magnitude 8 or 9 quake centered on the troff at up to
50 to 90 percent, depending on the model, in the next 30 years.
In a worst case scenario, that could cause up to 298,000 deaths.
Anthony Kuhn in PR News, Seoul.
In Egypt, at least seven people are dead, more than 100 injured, after two trains collided
today south of Cairo.
Officials say one train crashed into the back of another, causing several carriages to derail
and fall down in embankment.
Dozens of ambulances were on the scene helping transport victims to hospitals in the area.
The president of the country has ordered an investigation into the cause of that crash.
Officials at a chimp sanctuary in Florida used a drone to get food to a chimp separated
from his enclosure by floodwaters from recent rains.
Officials say Caleb missed a few meals when he decided to stay outside, but the rest of
the chimps went indoors.
I'm Janine Herfs, NPR News, in Washington.
